subject: economics
topicDisplay: Theme 3 Business Behaviour And The Labour Market
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly predicts that:
options: Firms always engage in price wars
questions.explain: The kink implies rivals match price cuts but not rises, so firms avoid changing price, giving price rigidity.

questions.q: A key feature distinguishing monopolistic competition from perfect competition is:
options: A single firm in the market
Product differentiation giving a downward-sloping demand curve
questions.explain: In monopolistic competition firms sell differentiated products, giving each a downward-sloping demand curve.

questions.q: For a monopsonist, the marginal cost of labour curve lies above the supply (AC of labour) curve because:
options: Wages fall as more workers are hired
To hire one more worker, the firm must raise the wage paid to all workers
questions.explain: A monopsonist hiring an extra worker must pay a higher wage to that worker and to all existing workers, so marginal cost exceeds the average wage.

questions.q: In the short run, the law of diminishing marginal returns states that as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor:
options: Total product eventually falls from the start
questions.explain: Beyond a certain point, adding more variable input to a fixed input causes marginal product to fall.

questions.q: Third-degree price discrimination requires the firm to:
options: Set price equal to marginal cost
Charge every consumer the same price
Separate markets with different price elasticities and prevent resale
questions.explain: Price discrimination needs market power, separable sub-markets with differing PED, and no arbitrage between them.

questions.q: Which of the following would increase a country's measured income inequality (a higher Gini)?
options: A widening gap between the highest and lowest earners
A rise in the minimum wage that compresses pay
questions.explain: A larger gap between top and bottom incomes bows the Lorenz curve further from equality and raises the Gini coefficient.

questions.q: A merger between a car manufacturer and a tyre producer is an example of:
questions.explain: A firm merging with a supplier earlier in its supply chain is backward vertical integration.

questions.q: Maturity transformation by banks refers to the practice of:
options: lending long-term while funding themselves with short-term deposits
converting foreign currency into domestic currency
questions.explain: Banks borrow short (deposits) and lend long, creating maturity mismatch and exposing them to liquidity risk.

questions.q: A key cause of the 2008 financial crisis was the:
options: sharp fall in global interest rates before 2007
mispricing of risk and growth of subprime mortgage-backed securities
excessive holding of cash reserves by banks
questions.explain: Risk was systematically underpriced as subprime loans were securitised and spread through the system, fuelling the crisis.

questions.q: Government policies to reduce inequality include:
options: Cutting the top rate of income tax
questions.explain: Progressive taxes take a larger share from higher earners while benefits and transfers raise lower incomes, narrowing the income distribution.

questions.q: X-inefficiency arises when a firm:
options: Operates with higher average costs than necessary due to lack of competitive pressure
questions.explain: X-inefficiency is the failure to minimise costs, often because monopoly power removes the pressure to be efficient.

questions.q: If a firm pursues revenue maximisation rather than profit maximisation, it produces where:
questions.explain: Total revenue is maximised where marginal revenue equals zero.

questions.q: Net migration of skilled workers into a country will tend to:
options: Always raise wages for all workers
Have no effect on the labour market
Shift labour supply right and reduce upward wage pressure in affected occupations
questions.explain: An inflow of workers increases labour supply, shifting the supply curve right and easing wage growth where they compete.

questions.q: Collective bargaining refers to:
options: Trade unions negotiating pay and conditions with employers on behalf of members
Individual workers negotiating their own pay
questions.explain: Collective bargaining is the process by which unions negotiate wages and working conditions for a group of workers, increasing their bargaining power.

questions.q: A monopolist that practises first-degree (perfect) price discrimination:
options: Charges every consumer their maximum willingness to pay, capturing all consumer surplus
questions.explain: Perfect price discrimination charges each consumer their reservation price, converting all consumer surplus into profit.

questions.q: A firm experiences increasing returns to scale when:
options: Output rises proportionately less than inputs
Output rises proportionately more than all inputs
Output stays constant as inputs rise
questions.explain: Increasing returns to scale occur when a given proportional increase in all inputs yields a larger proportional rise in output.

questions.q: The principal-agent problem in the theory of the firm refers to:
options: A conflict between consumers and producers
A divergence of objectives between owners (principals) and managers (agents)
questions.explain: Separation of ownership and control means managers may pursue their own goals rather than maximising owner profit.

questions.q: A national minimum wage set above the market equilibrium in a competitive labour market is likely to cause:
questions.explain: Above equilibrium, the quantity of labour supplied exceeds the quantity demanded, creating a surplus of workers, i.e. unemployment.

questions.q: A monopsony in the labour market is:
options: A market with many competing employers
questions.explain: A monopsony is a market with a single dominant buyer (employer) of labour, giving it wage-setting power.

questions.q: In a monopsony, the firm's marginal revenue product curve represents its:
questions.explain: The MRP curve shows the value of each additional worker and therefore acts as the firm's demand curve for labour.

questions.q: Allocative efficiency is achieved at the level of output where:
questions.explain: Allocative efficiency occurs where P=MC, so the value consumers place on the last unit equals its production cost.

questions.q: Compared with a competitive labour market, a profit-maximising monopsonist tends to:
options: Always pay above the marginal revenue product
Employ more workers at a higher wage
Employ fewer workers at a lower wage
Employ the same workers at the same wage
questions.explain: Because the marginal cost of labour lies above the supply curve, the monopsonist restricts employment and pays a wage below MRP.

questions.q: Barriers to entry that protect a monopoly include:
options: Patents, high sunk costs and economies of scale
questions.explain: Patents, large sunk costs and scale advantages deter new firms, sustaining a monopolist's market power.

questions.q: Which factor would shift the demand for labour curve to the right?
options: An increase in the demand for the firm's product
A fall in the price of the product
An increase in capital that substitutes for labour
A rise in the wage rate
questions.explain: Since labour demand is derived, a rise in product demand raises MRP and shifts the labour demand curve rightward.

questions.q: For a perfectly competitive firm, the demand curve it faces is:
options: Perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price
questions.explain: A price-taking firm faces a horizontal, perfectly elastic demand curve at the prevailing market price.

questions.q: The information failure where the party with more knowledge (e.g. a borrower) has an advantage over the lender is called:
questions.explain: Asymmetric information describes one party (the borrower) knowing more about the risk than the other (the lender).

questions.q: In a perfectly competitive labour market, an individual firm faces a labour supply curve that is:
options: Perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market wage
questions.explain: A single firm is a wage-taker and can hire as many workers as it wishes at the going market wage, so its supply of labour is perfectly elastic.

questions.q: A bilateral monopoly in the labour market exists when:
options: A single worker faces many employers
A monopsony employer bargains with a monopoly trade union
questions.explain: A bilateral monopoly arises when a single buyer (monopsony) negotiates with a single seller (a monopoly union), so the wage is set by bargaining.

questions.q: The supply of labour to a particular occupation is likely to be more elastic when:
options: Few skills or qualifications are needed and there is a large pool of available workers
questions.explain: Where little training is needed and workers can move into the job easily, labour supply responds readily to wage changes, i.e. it is elastic.

questions.q: Dynamic efficiency refers to:
options: Producing at minimum average cost today
Setting price equal to marginal cost
Improvements in efficiency over time through investment and innovation
questions.explain: Dynamic efficiency concerns efficiency gains over time via investment, research and innovation.
